findings.summary: CRLF in a message subject injects arbitrary headers (email header injection, CWE-93)
findings.description:
## Affected

`github.com/malcolmston/nodemailer` `<= v0.0.0-20260810111553-311143ed3171`, `Message.SetSubject`. Parity case **`subject-with-newline`** (`parity/nodemailer/cases/subject.json`), recorded as divergence **2** ("Header injection through `subject`") in `parity/nodemailer/COVERAGE.md`. Upstream oracle: `nodemailer@6.9.16`.

## Upstream vs port behaviour

`Message.SetSubject` writes the supplied value into the `Subject:` header **verbatim**, CRLF included. A subject containing `\r\n` therefore terminates the header field, and everything after it becomes a new header field of the composed message.

Given the subject `"Innocent\r\nX-Injected: yes"`:

| | composed message |
| --- | --- |
| upstream 6.9.16 | one header: `Subject: Innocent X-Injected: yes` — the CRLF is folded into the subject value, so the payload stays *inside* the field |
| this port | two headers: `Subject: Innocent` **and a real `X-Injected: yes` header** |

The harness canonicaliser parses both messages with the same parser, so this appears as a genuine extra header on the Go side, not as a formatting artefact.

## Impact

This is the classic email-header-injection sink (CWE-93). Subjects are frequently attacker- or user-controlled: ticket titles, "someone commented: <their text>", order references, search terms echoed back in a notification. Any such value reaching `SetSubject` lets the submitter write arbitrary message headers, which is enough to:

- add `Bcc:` or extra `To:` recipients and exfiltrate the message body — typically containing a password-reset link, an invoice, or account data — to an address of their choosing;
- overwrite `Reply-To` and adjacent fields to redirect replies;
- inject a blank line and therefore an entire forged body / MIME structure after the header block.

Graded moderate rather than high because exploitation requires the embedding application to pass untrusted input through to a subject (or another header value); the library on its own is not remotely reachable. Where that data flow exists, impact is significant.

RFC 5322 forbids bare CR/LF in a field value at all, so no legitimate input is broken by fixing this.

## Repro

```go
m := nodemailer.NewMessage()
m.SetFrom("a@example.com")
m.AddTo("b@example.com")
m.SetSubject("Innocent\r\nX-Injected: yes")
m.SetText("hello")
b, _ := m.Build()
fmt.Printf("%s", b)   // output contains a line "X-Injected: yes"
```

Harness: `cd parity/nodemailer/node && npm install && cd .. && GOWORK=off go test ./...`

## Fix

Sanitise before encoding, in `SetSubject` and in **every** other header-value path — `AddHeader`, display names, `Message-ID`, `In-Reply-To`, `References`, attachment filenames. Strip or fold bare `\r` and `\n`. Upstream folds: replace the CRLF with a fold (CRLF + WSP) or a single space so the payload remains inside the field value; that also keeps parity. Returning an error would be defensible, but folding matches upstream. A single shared header-value sanitiser applied at the encoding boundary is preferable to per-setter checks, so future setters cannot reintroduce the sink.
